endorsements.quote: These experiences underscore the urgent need for mandatory post-market surveillance, transparent error-reporting mechanisms, and robust bias-mitigation strategies before broad clinical deployment.
Licensing standards for AI-driven medical devices – AI systems should be subject to approval requirements that assess accuracy, fairness and transparency before clinical deployment.
Consequently, AI-based clinical decision-support systems fall within the ambit of services requiring informed consent.[21]
Rather, it must form part of an overarching health innovation plan that contemplates phased integration, ongoing training of personnel, infrastructure upgrades, and monitoring of outcomes.
Given the likelihood that South African courts will need to balance professional accountability with the need for innovation, statutory guidance on AI liability is urgently needed.

unlisted_practices: Regulators should require periodic mandatory bias audits of AI models to detect and mitigate discriminatory outcomes in medical decision-making.
Design AI-driven medical tools with interpretability mechanisms so providers and patients can understand and challenge algorithmic decisions.
Professional regulators should expand ethical codes to define physicians' responsibilities when using AI in patient care.
Professional regulators should require explainability training and algorithmic bias audits for practitioners using AI.
Policymakers should implement technology transfer initiatives and public-sector funding so AI tools are deployed across both private and public hospitals.

Calibrate regulatory oversight intensity to AI risk, with high-risk systems requiring pre-market approval, ongoing bias and fairness audits, mandatory explainability reports, and post-market surveillance.
Regulators should clarify re-certification requirements for adaptive AI models and adapt adverse-event reporting to algorithm-specific failure modes such as concept drift.
